questions.stem: A 45-year-old man reports several weeks of epigastric burning. Endoscopy reveals a duodenal ulcer. Of the following, which pair represents the two most common causes of peptic ulcer disease overall?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Helicobacter pylori infection and NSAID use

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bile reflux and autoimmune parietal cell destruction

explanation.summary: H. pylori is the leading cause of PUD, with NSAIDs second.
explanation.whyCorrect: H. pylori infection is the most common cause of peptic ulcer disease and chronic gastritis, and NSAID use is the second most common cause; together they account for the overwhelming majority of ulcers.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alcohol and smoking are contributing risk factors but are not the two leading causes; alcohol is a cause of gastritis, not an independent cause of PUD.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Bile reflux and autoimmune destruction cause gastritis but are uncommon causes of frank peptic ulceration.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is a rare cause, and stress alone is not a leading cause of chronic PUD.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Corticosteroids modestly increase ulcer risk mainly with NSAIDs, and viral gastroenteritis does not cause PUD.

questions.stem: A gram-negative curved rod colonizes the gastric mucosa despite the low luminal pH. Which mechanism best explains how this organism survives the acidic gastric environment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It burrows deep into the submucosa away from acid

choices.label: C
choices.text: It produces urease that generates a base to raise local pH

choices.label: D
choices.text: It secretes bicarbonate directly from a membrane pump

choices.label: E
choices.text: It coats itself in a thick lipopolysaccharide capsule impervious to acid

explanation.summary: H. pylori urease neutralizes surrounding acid.
explanation.whyCorrect: H. pylori produces urease, which hydrolyzes urea into ammonium carbonate, a base that raises the local pH and creates a neutralized microenvironment allowing the bacterium to survive on the gastric mucosa.

whyWrongByChoice.A: H. pylori survives on or within the mucus layer and does not invade the submucosa.
whyWrongByChoice.B: H. pylori does not form spores.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The bacterium does not secrete bicarbonate; it generates ammonia via urease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An LPS capsule does not neutralize gastric acid; urease-generated base does.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man describes epigastric pain that awakens him at night and is relieved within minutes of eating a snack. Which type of ulcer and mechanism best explains this pattern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Duodenal ulcer; food transiently buffers acid and pain improves with eating

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gastric ulcer; food stimulates acid against the ulcer so pain worsens with eating

choices.label: C
choices.text: Esophageal ulcer; supine acid reflux triggers pain only when upright

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stress ulcer; splanchnic vasoconstriction causes fasting pain

choices.label: E
choices.text: Malignant gastric ulcer; pain is unrelated to meals

explanation.summary: Duodenal ulcer pain classically improves with food and occurs at night.
explanation.whyCorrect: Duodenal ulcer pain characteristically improves with eating because food and gastric emptying transiently buffer duodenal acid, and pain often recurs at night when the stomach is empty.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Gastric ulcer pain classically worsens with eating, which is the opposite of this presentation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Esophageal ulcer pain relates to reflux and swallowing, not relief with food and nocturnal timing.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Stress ulcers occur in critically ill patients and present with bleeding, not this classic meal-related pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Malignant ulcers do not produce this reproducible food-relieved, nocturnal pattern.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman has multiple recurrent ulcers extending beyond the first part of the duodenum, chronic watery diarrhea, and a markedly elevated fasting serum gastrin with gastric pH below 2. Which underlying process is most likely responsible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoimmune destruction of parietal cells in the gastric body

choices.label: B
choices.text: H. pylori antral inflammation increasing acid secretion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Bile reflux following prior gastric surgery

explanation.summary: Refractory distal ulcers plus diarrhea and high gastrin indicate a gastrinoma (ZES).
explanation.whyCorrect: Multiple/refractory ulcers in atypical (distal) locations, secretory diarrhea, and markedly elevated fasting gastrin with very low gastric pH describe Zollinger-Ellison syndrome caused by a gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumor (gastrinoma).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autoimmune gastritis destroys parietal cells causing hypochlorhydria and high gastrin but with high, not low, gastric pH and no acid-driven distal ulcers.
whyWrongByChoice.B: H. pylori raises acid modestly but does not produce gastrin levels 10 times normal or ulcers distal to the duodenal bulb.
whyWrongByChoice.C: NSAID ulcers are not associated with hypergastrinemia or secretory diarrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bile reflux causes gastritis with bilious vomiting, not hypergastrinemia and refractory distal ulcers.

questions.stem: A patient with recurrent ulcers has a borderline fasting serum gastrin, and Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is suspected. Which test result would best confirm the diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A low gastric pH measured alone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Free air under the diaphragm on upright X-ray

choices.label: D
choices.text: A drop in gastrin after an oral glucose load

choices.label: E
choices.text: A paradoxical rise in serum gastrin after intravenous secretin

explanation.summary: Secretin paradoxically raises gastrin in gastrinoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: In Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, intravenous secretin paradoxically stimulates gastrinoma cells to release more gastrin, causing a marked rise, whereas normal G cells would be inhibited; this confirms the diagnosis when gastrin is borderline.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Low gastric pH is expected in ZES but is nonspecific and does not confirm a gastrinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The urea breath test detects H. pylori, not a gastrinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Free air indicates perforation, not ZES.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An oral glucose load tests for insulin/growth hormone disorders, not gastrinoma.

questions.stem: A patient with confirmed Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is being localized for surgery. Approximately 90% of gastrinomas are found in which anatomic region?

choices.label: B
choices.text: The gastrinoma triangle, involving the duodenum and head of the pancreas

choices.label: C
choices.text: The distal ileum and terminal small bowel

choices.label: E
choices.text: The splenic hilum and tail of the pancreas

explanation.summary: Most gastrinomas lie in the gastrinoma triangle.
explanation.whyCorrect: About 90% of gastrinomas are located in the gastrinoma triangle, bounded by the cystic/common bile duct junction, the second-third portion of the duodenum, and the neck-body junction of the pancreas.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The gastric fundus is not the typical site; it houses parietal cells, not gastrinomas.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The distal ileum is not part of the gastrinoma triangle.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The gastroesophageal junction is not a common gastrinoma location.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Most gastrinomas are in the triangle near the head of the pancreas, not the tail/splenic hilum.

questions.stem: During endoscopy, a clinician identifies an ulcer along the gastric body. Compared with a duodenal ulcer, which management step is specifically indicated for this gastric ulcer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No further evaluation because gastric ulcers are always benign

choices.label: B
choices.text: Immediate surgical resection of the stomach

choices.label: C
choices.text: Biopsy of the ulcer to rule out malignancy

explanation.summary: Gastric ulcers require biopsy to exclude malignancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gastric ulcers carry a risk of underlying carcinoma, so biopsy is required to rule out malignancy, whereas duodenal ulcers are generally benign and do not routinely require biopsy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gastric ulcers are not always benign; carcinoma must be excluded.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Surgery is not indicated before biopsy; most ulcers are managed medically.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Secretin testing is for suspected gastrinoma, not routine gastric ulcers.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Endoscopy is superior to barium swallow because it allows the needed biopsy.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old presents with epigastric pain and suspected peptic ulcer disease. Which is the diagnostic modality of choice?

explanation.summary: EGD is the diagnostic test of choice for PUD.
explanation.whyCorrect: Esophagogastroduodenoscopy directly visualizes the ulcer, permits biopsy to exclude malignancy, and allows H. pylori testing, making it the diagnostic tool of choice for peptic ulcer disease.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Barium swallow is less sensitive and cannot obtain biopsy or treat bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ultrasound does not visualize mucosal ulcers.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The urea breath test detects H. pylori but does not diagnose or characterize the ulcer.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serum gastrin is used for suspected gastrinoma, not routine PUD diagnosis.

questions.stem: A gastric biopsy is placed into a phenol red-containing reagent as part of a rapid urease (CLO) test. A positive result for H. pylori is indicated by which color change?

explanation.summary: Urease raises pH, turning phenol red from yellow to red.
explanation.whyCorrect: H. pylori urease hydrolyzes urea to ammonium carbonate, raising the local pH; this alkaline shift turns the phenol red indicator from yellow (negative) to red/pink (positive).

whyWrongByChoice.A: The change is from yellow to red, not red to yellow.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Phenol red does not shift blue to green.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The reagent does not turn clear to purple.
whyWrongByChoice.E: There is no green-to-colorless transition in this test.

questions.stem: A patient with an H. pylori-negative NSAID-associated ulcer needs pharmacologic therapy to promote ulcer healing. Which drug class is first-line for ulcer healing?

explanation.summary: PPIs are first-line for ulcer healing.
explanation.whyCorrect: Proton pump inhibitors most effectively and durably block gastric H+/K+-ATPase, producing the least-acidic environment and the highest ulcer healing rates, making them first-line therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antacids provide symptomatic relief but do not heal ulcers as effectively as PPIs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: H2 blockers reduce acid but are less potent than PPIs for healing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anticholinergics are not first-line and cause many side effects.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prostaglandin analogs (misoprostol) are used mainly for prophylaxis, not as first-line healing agents.

questions.stem: A patient with a known duodenal ulcer suddenly develops massive hematemesis and hemodynamic instability. A posteriorly located ulcer in the first part of the duodenum most likely eroded which vessel?

explanation.summary: Posterior duodenal ulcers erode the gastroduodenal artery.
explanation.whyCorrect: The gastroduodenal artery runs directly behind the first part of the duodenum, so a posterior duodenal ulcer can erode into it and cause severe, life-threatening hemorrhage.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The left gastric artery supplies the lesser curvature and is not behind the duodenal bulb.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The splenic artery runs along the pancreas toward the spleen, not behind the duodenal bulb.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The SMA is not the vessel classically eroded by a posterior duodenal ulcer.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Short gastric arteries supply the gastric fundus, far from the duodenum.

questions.stem: A man with a long history of ulcer symptoms develops sudden severe, sharp abdominal pain with a rigid, board-like abdomen. Upright chest X-ray shows free air under the diaphragm. Which complication has occurred?

explanation.summary: Free air with a rigid abdomen indicates perforation.
explanation.whyCorrect: A full-thickness perforation allows air and gastric contents into the peritoneal cavity, producing acute sharp pain, a rigid abdomen (peritonitis), and free air under the diaphragm on upright chest X-ray in about 85% of cases.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bleeding presents with hematemesis or melena, not free intraperitoneal air.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gastric outlet obstruction causes vomiting and early satiety, not free air.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pernicious anemia is a chronic B12-deficiency complication, not an acute surgical abdomen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Malignant transformation does not produce acute free air and peritonitis.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman has fatigue, paresthesias, and a macrocytic anemia. Workup shows anti-parietal cell antibodies and low vitamin B12. Which process best explains her condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoimmune destruction of parietal cells causing loss of intrinsic factor

choices.label: B
choices.text: H. pylori antral infection increasing acid output

choices.label: E
choices.text: Bile reflux irritating the gastric mucosa

explanation.summary: Autoimmune gastritis destroys parietal cells, causing B12 deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Autoimmune (type A) gastritis features immune destruction of parietal cells in the body and fundus with anti-parietal cell and anti-intrinsic-factor antibodies; loss of intrinsic factor impairs B12 absorption, producing pernicious (megaloblastic) anemia and neurologic symptoms.

whyWrongByChoice.B: H. pylori antral gastritis raises acid and causes ulcers, not intrinsic factor loss and B12 deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: NSAIDs deplete prostaglandins and injure mucosa but do not cause autoantibody-mediated B12 deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A gastrinoma causes acid hypersecretion and ulcers, not pernicious anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bile reflux causes gastritis with bilious vomiting, not B12 deficiency from parietal cell autoantibodies.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman on chronic ibuprofen for arthritis develops a gastric ulcer. Which mechanism best explains how her medication predisposed her to ulceration?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Direct stimulation of gastrin release from antral G cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased urease activity in the gastric mucosa

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibition of cyclooxygenase, reducing protective prostaglandins

choices.label: E
choices.text: Paradoxical increase in mucosal bicarbonate secretion

explanation.summary: NSAIDs inhibit COX, lowering protective prostaglandins.
explanation.whyCorrect: NSAIDs inhibit cyclooxygenase, decreasing prostaglandin E2, which normally stimulates mucus and bicarbonate secretion, maintains mucosal blood flow, and promotes epithelial repair; loss of these defenses allows acid injury and ulceration.

whyWrongByChoice.A: NSAIDs do not cause ulcers by stimulating gastrin release.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Parietal cell destruction is autoimmune gastritis, unrelated to NSAID mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Urease is an H. pylori enzyme, not an effect of NSAIDs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: NSAIDs decrease, not increase, bicarbonate secretion by lowering prostaglandins.

questions.stem: A patient in the neurosurgical ICU with elevated intracranial pressure after a traumatic brain injury develops an acute gastric stress ulcer. This lesion is best described by which eponym?

explanation.summary: Stress ulcers from raised intracranial pressure are Cushing ulcers.
explanation.whyCorrect: A Cushing ulcer is a stress ulcer associated with raised intracranial pressure (e.g., brain injury), thought to reflect increased vagal stimulation and acid secretion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A Curling ulcer is a stress ulcer associated with severe burns, not intracranial pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A Dieulafoy lesion is an abnormal large submucosal artery, not a stress ulcer.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A Cameron lesion is an erosion within a hiatal hernia, unrelated to ICP.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A Marjolin ulcer is a malignancy arising in chronic wounds or scars, not a gastric stress ulcer.

questions.stem: A patient with an H. pylori-positive duodenal ulcer is started on bismuth-based quadruple therapy. Which combination correctly lists the components of this regimen?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Amoxicillin, clarithromycin, ciprofloxacin, and an antacid

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bismuth, metronidazole, tetracycline, and a proton pump inhibitor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bismuth, azithromycin, rifaximin, and an H2 blocker

choices.label: E
choices.text: Clarithromycin, amoxicillin, octreotide, and a proton pump inhibitor

explanation.summary: Quadruple therapy is bismuth, metronidazole, tetracycline, and a PPI.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bismuth-based quadruple therapy for H. pylori consists of bismuth subsalicylate, metronidazole, tetracycline, and a proton pump inhibitor, given for 10-14 days.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This combination is incorrect and omits bismuth and a PPI while adding an antacid.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Azithromycin and rifaximin are not part of standard quadruple therapy, and a PPI, not an H2 blocker, is used.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Doxycycline cannot substitute for tetracycline due to resistance, and sucralfate/misoprostol are not part of the regimen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Octreotide is not an H. pylori agent; this is not the quadruple regimen.

questions.stem: An H. pylori strain injects a protein into gastric epithelial cells that disrupts tight junctions and the cytoskeleton and drives inflammation, correlating with more severe disease. Which virulence factor is described?

explanation.summary: CagA is injected into epithelial cells and disrupts tight junctions.
explanation.whyCorrect: CagA is translocated into gastric epithelial cells where it disrupts tight junctions and the cytoskeleton and promotes inflammation, correlating with more severe disease including ulcers and cancer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Urease neutralizes acid to allow survival; it is not injected to disrupt the cytoskeleton.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The flagellum provides motility for penetrating mucus, not intracellular injection of a toxin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: VacA acts extracellularly to form vacuoles and induce apoptosis, rather than being injected to disrupt tight junctions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: LPS contributes to inflammation but is not the injected effector described.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic duodenal ulcer disease presents with recurrent vomiting of undigested food, early satiety, and a succussion splash on exam. Which complication is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Gastric outlet obstruction from inflammation and scarring near the pylorus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pernicious anemia from intrinsic factor loss

choices.label: E
choices.text: MALT lymphoma of the gastric antrum

explanation.summary: Vomiting undigested food and succussion splash indicate gastric outlet obstruction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chronic peri-pyloric duodenal ulceration leads to inflammation, fibrosis, and scarring that narrows the outlet, producing gastric outlet obstruction with vomiting of undigested food, early satiety, and a succussion splash.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Perforation causes acute severe pain and peritonitis, not chronic obstructive vomiting.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Arterial erosion causes hemorrhage, not obstructive symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pernicious anemia is a chronic hematologic/neurologic problem, not mechanical obstruction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MALT lymphoma causes chronic dyspepsia but not this classic obstructive picture.

questions.stem: Two patients are colonized with H. pylori. One has antral-predominant infection and the other has body (corpus)-predominant infection. Which statement best contrasts their expected ulcer patterns?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antral-predominant infection weakens defenses and causes gastric ulcers

choices.label: B
choices.text: Body-predominant infection increases acid output and causes duodenal ulcers

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both patterns eliminate acid secretion and prevent any ulcers

choices.label: D
choices.text: Antral-predominant infection increases acid and favors duodenal ulcers, while body-predominant infection weakens defenses and favors gastric ulcers

choices.label: E
choices.text: Body-predominant infection has no effect on ulcer location

explanation.summary: Antral-predominant favors duodenal ulcers; body-predominant favors gastric ulcers.
explanation.whyCorrect: Antral-predominant H. pylori increases gastrin and acid secretion, promoting duodenal ulcers, whereas body (corpus)-predominant infection damages acid-secreting mucosa and weakens defenses, promoting gastric ulcers and atrophy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This reverses the relationship; antral-predominant infection increases acid and favors duodenal ulcers.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This reverses the relationship; body-predominant infection weakens defenses and favors gastric ulcers.
whyWrongByChoice.C: H. pylori does not uniformly eliminate acid and prevent ulcers.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Body-predominant infection does influence ulcer location, favoring gastric ulcers.

questions.stem: After completing quadruple therapy for an H. pylori-associated ulcer, a patient returns to confirm that eradication was successful. Which test is preferred to confirm eradication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Serum anti-H. pylori IgG antibody titer

explanation.summary: The urea breath test is preferred to confirm H. pylori eradication.
explanation.whyCorrect: The urea breath test is noninvasive, accurate, and reflects active infection, making it the preferred method to confirm eradication after therapy; testing should follow appropriate PPI and antibiotic washout to avoid false negatives.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Serologic IgG remains positive long after eradication and cannot confirm cure.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Serum gastrin evaluates for gastrinoma, not H. pylori eradication.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Barium swallow does not detect active H. pylori infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A CBC assesses anemia but does not confirm eradication of the organism.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man undergoes upper endoscopy for chronic dyspepsia. Multiple small, smooth, dome-shaped polyps are seen in a background of inflamed, atrophic mucosa. Biopsy of one polyp shows foveolar hyperplasia with edematous, inflamed stroma and no dysplasia. Which of the following is the most likely type of gastric polyp?

explanation.summary: Hyperplastic polyps are the most common gastric polyp and arise from chronic inflammation.
explanation.whyCorrect: About 75% of gastric polyps are hyperplastic. They arise in the setting of chronic gastritis, are usually small dome-shaped nodules of foveolar hyperplasia with inflamed stroma, and carry low malignant potential.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adenomas are dysplastic premalignant lesions and account for only about 10% of gastric polyps; this biopsy shows no dysplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fundic gland polyps arise from proton pump inhibitor use or polyposis syndromes, not from atrophic inflamed mucosa with foveolar hyperplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A GIST is a submucosal mesenchymal tumor of interstitial cells of Cajal, not a mucosal foveolar polyp.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Signet ring cell carcinoma is a malignant diffuse-type cancer, not a benign inflammatory polyp.

questions.stem: During endoscopy, a flat lesion is biopsied from the gastric antrum of a 60-year-old woman with a history of chronic gastritis. Histology shows elongated, hyperchromatic, crowded columnar cells with intestinal metaplasia and low-grade dysplasia. Which feature best explains why this lesion has greater malignant potential than a hyperplastic polyp?

explanation.summary: Gastric adenomas are dysplastic by definition, making them premalignant.
explanation.whyCorrect: Adenomas contain dysplastic epithelium, meaning the cells have lost normal architecture and maturation. This premalignant change is why all gastric adenomas are resected, unlike usually benign hyperplastic polyps.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Size increases risk within a lesion type but is not the defining reason adenomas are premalignant; dysplasia is intrinsic to them.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antral location is common for adenomas but does not itself confer malignant potential.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inflamed foveolar epithelium describes hyperplastic polyps, which have low malignant potential.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pedunculated shape is not the feature responsible for the adenoma's premalignant nature.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man presents with epigastric pain, weight loss, and iron-deficiency anemia. Endoscopy reveals an exophytic ulcerated mass in the antrum, and biopsy shows malignant cells forming irregular glands. Which of the following is the single most common malignancy of the stomach?

explanation.summary: Adenocarcinoma is the most common gastric malignancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gastric adenocarcinoma accounts for more than 90% of all gastric cancers. The gland-forming, exophytic antral mass described is the classic intestinal-type adenocarcinoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: MALT lymphoma accounts for only about 5% of gastric malignancies.
whyWrongByChoice.C: GISTs are mesenchymal tumors and far less common than adenocarcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumors are relatively uncommon gastric malignancies.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Leiomyosarcoma is a rare smooth muscle malignancy of the stomach.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman presents with early satiety and weight loss. Endoscopy shows a rigid, thickened stomach wall with loss of rugal folds and no dominant mass. Biopsy reveals infiltrating cells with large mucin vacuoles displacing the nucleus to the periphery. Which of the following best describes this tumor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Intestinal-type adenocarcinoma arising from an adenoma

choices.label: C
choices.text: Marginal zone B-cell lymphoma with lymphoepithelial lesions

choices.label: D
choices.text: Diffuse-type adenocarcinoma with signet ring cells (linitis plastica)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spindle cell mesenchymal tumor forming whorls

explanation.summary: Signet ring cells with a leather-bottle stomach define diffuse-type gastric cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: Diffuse-type adenocarcinoma grows infiltratively as signet ring cells with desmoplasia, producing the stiff, thickened linitis plastica ('leather bottle') stomach with loss of rugal folds and no focal mass. It often occurs in younger patients of either sex.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Intestinal-type cancer forms glands, is typically an exophytic distal mass, and arises from adenomas; diffuse-type has no precursor lesion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A well-differentiated gland-forming exophytic mass describes intestinal-type, not the infiltrative signet ring pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MALT lymphoma shows lymphoepithelial lesions from B-cell infiltration, not signet ring cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Spindle cell whorls describe a GIST, a mesenchymal tumor, not an epithelial signet ring cancer.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with long-standing H. pylori infection is diagnosed with gastric adenocarcinoma. Which specific H. pylori virulence factor is most closely associated with the development of adenocarcinoma?

explanation.summary: CagA-positive H. pylori strains are most linked to adenocarcinoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Strains carrying CagA inject the cytotoxin-associated gene product into epithelial cells, triggering signaling cascades that result in unregulated cell growth, and are strongly linked to gastric adenocarcinoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Urease neutralizes gastric acid to allow colonization but is not the factor specifically tied to carcinogenesis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Flagellar motility aids colonization of the mucus layer but is not the oncogenic driver.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Biofilm formation aids persistence but is not the key carcinogenic virulence factor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lipopolysaccharide contributes to inflammation but CagA is the factor most associated with cancer.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with gastric adenocarcinoma is found on exam to have a firm, enlarged lymph node in the left supraclavicular fossa. This node is most appropriately termed which of the following?

explanation.summary: The left supraclavicular sentinel node of gastric cancer is the Virchow node.
explanation.whyCorrect: The Virchow node is the left supraclavicular sentinel lymph node metastasis of advanced gastric cancer.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A Krukenberg tumor is metastatic gastric cancer to the ovaries, not a supraclavicular node.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A Sister Mary Joseph nodule is a periumbilical metastasis, not a supraclavicular node.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Blumer shelf refers to a rectal shelf from drop metastases in the pelvis, not a supraclavicular node.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An Irish node refers to a left axillary node, not the left supraclavicular node.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with epigastric pain and weight loss. Endoscopic biopsy shows a dense infiltrate of small monoclonal B cells that invade and destroy gastric glands, forming lymphoepithelial lesions. H. pylori organisms are identified. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

explanation.summary: H. pylori eradication cures most gastric MALT lymphomas.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gastric MALT lymphoma is an indolent H. pylori-driven marginal zone B-cell tumor. Eradicating H. pylori achieves complete remission in about 75% of cases and is first-line therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Total gastrectomy is not first-line for H. pylori-associated MALT lymphoma, which often regresses with antibiotics.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rituximab-based chemotherapy is reserved for lymphomas that fail to regress after eradication or lack H. pylori.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Radiation is used for localized disease not responding to eradication, not as first-line.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Imatinib treats GISTs by inhibiting KIT/PDGFRA and has no role in MALT lymphoma.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man has a 6 cm submucosal mass in the gastric body. Biopsy shows spindle cells arranged in whorls and fascicles with eosinophilic cytoplasm. Immunohistochemistry is strongly positive for KIT (CD117). From which cell type does this tumor most likely arise?

explanation.summary: GISTs arise from interstitial cells of Cajal and are KIT-positive.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gastrointestinal stromal tumors arise from interstitial cells of Cajal (the GI pacemaker cells) and are driven by KIT or PDGFRA gain-of-function mutations, hence CD117/KIT positivity and spindle cell morphology.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Parietal cells secrete acid and intrinsic factor and are not the origin of GISTs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chief cells secrete pepsinogen and are epithelial, not the source of mesenchymal GISTs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Marginal zone B cells give rise to MALT lymphoma, not KIT-positive spindle cell tumors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Foveolar epithelial cells give rise to hyperplastic polyps and adenocarcinoma, not GISTs.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man has an unresectable gastric GIST with a documented KIT gain-of-function mutation. Which of the following best explains why imatinib is effective in this tumor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It eradicates H. pylori and removes the inflammatory stimulus

choices.label: B
choices.text: It depletes malignant B cells via CD20 binding

choices.label: D
choices.text: It inhibits the tyrosine kinase receptors driving tumor growth

explanation.summary: Imatinib inhibits the KIT/PDGFRA tyrosine kinases that drive GISTs.
explanation.whyCorrect: GIST growth depends on gain-of-function mutations in tyrosine kinase receptors (KIT and PDGFRA). Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor that blocks these receptors, halting tumor proliferation, and is used for unresectable, recurrent, or metastatic GISTs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: H. pylori eradication treats MALT lymphoma, not GIST; imatinib is not an antibiotic.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD20-directed therapy (rituximab) targets B-cell lymphomas, not KIT-driven GISTs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Imatinib does not restore TP53 function; it inhibits tyrosine kinases.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Imatinib does not act on E-cadherin, which is relevant to diffuse-type adenocarcinoma.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old woman with a strong family history of gastric cancer is found to have diffuse-type gastric adenocarcinoma with signet ring cells. Germline mutation in which gene, encoding a cell adhesion protein, is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: CDH1 (E-cadherin) loss underlies hereditary diffuse gastric cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: CDH1 encodes E-cadherin, a cell adhesion molecule. Loss of E-cadherin function impairs cell adhesion and is central to diffuse-type gastric cancer; about 50% of diffuse tumors carry CDH1 mutations, and germline mutations cause hereditary diffuse gastric cancer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: KIT mutations drive GISTs, not diffuse-type adenocarcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: APC mutations cause familial adenomatous polyposis, which predisposes to intestinal-type (not diffuse-type) gastric cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.C: TP53 is a tumor suppressor commonly mutated in many cancers but is not the E-cadherin adhesion gene of hereditary diffuse gastric cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PDGFRA mutations drive a subset of GISTs, not diffuse gastric adenocarcinoma.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman with gastric adenocarcinoma is found on pelvic ultrasound to have bilateral solid ovarian masses. Biopsy shows mucin-filled signet ring cells within the ovarian stroma. Which of the following best describes this finding?

explanation.summary: Metastatic signet ring gastric cancer to the ovaries is a Krukenberg tumor.
explanation.whyCorrect: A Krukenberg tumor is metastatic gastric cancer to the ovaries, classically bilateral and composed of mucin-filled signet ring cells within the ovarian stroma.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A Virchow node is a left supraclavicular lymph node metastasis, not an ovarian lesion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A Sister Mary Joseph nodule is a periumbilical metastasis, not ovarian.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A primary ovarian mucinous cystadenocarcinoma arises in the ovary itself; here the signet ring cells are metastatic from the stomach.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Meigs syndrome is a benign ovarian fibroma with ascites and pleural effusion, not metastatic signet ring cells.

questions.stem: An endoscopist evaluates several gastric polyps in a 64-year-old patient. Which single feature makes a hyperplastic polyp significantly more likely to harbor malignancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sessile shape and size under 1 cm

choices.label: B
choices.text: Size greater than 1.5 cm and pedunculated

explanation.summary: Larger, pedunculated hyperplastic polyps carry higher malignant risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: A hyperplastic polyp larger than 1.5 cm and pedunculated is significantly more likely to be malignant; the larger the polyp, the greater the risk of dysplasia and malignant transformation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Small (<1 cm) sessile polyps carry low malignant potential.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antral location alone does not significantly raise the malignant risk of a hyperplastic polyp.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dome-shaped morphology is the typical benign appearance and is not a marker of malignancy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Multiplicity of small polyps does not by itself indicate higher malignant potential; size and pedunculation matter.

questions.stem: A pathologist reviews a gastric biopsy of an indolent B-cell lymphoma. Which immunophenotype is most characteristic of MALT lymphoma cells?

choices.label: C
choices.text: CD19 and CD20 positive, CD5 and CD10 negative

explanation.summary: MALT lymphoma cells are mature B cells: CD19/CD20 positive, CD5/CD10 negative.
explanation.whyCorrect: As mature marginal zone B-cell tumors, MALT lymphomas express the B-cell markers CD19 and CD20, do not express CD5 or CD10, and are CD43-positive in about 25% of cases.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD5 and CD10 positivity would suggest other lymphomas (e.g., mantle cell or follicular); MALT lymphoma is negative for both.
whyWrongByChoice.B: KIT and PDGFRA are markers/drivers of GISTs, not B-cell lymphomas.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CD3 and CD4 are T-cell markers; MALT lymphoma is a B-cell neoplasm.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TP53 and CDH1 are tumor-related genes in adenocarcinoma, not surface markers of MALT lymphoma cells.

questions.stem: A researcher describes the stepwise histologic progression of H. pylori-driven intestinal-type gastric carcinogenesis. Which of the following sequences is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Normal mucosa → dysplasia → intestinal metaplasia → chronic gastritis → adenocarcinoma

choices.label: B
choices.text: Normal mucosa → intestinal metaplasia → chronic gastritis → dysplasia → adenocarcinoma

choices.label: C
choices.text: Normal mucosa → adenocarcinoma → dysplasia → intestinal metaplasia → chronic gastritis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Normal mucosa → chronic gastritis → intestinal metaplasia → dysplasia → adenocarcinoma

choices.label: E
choices.text: Normal mucosa → chronic gastritis → dysplasia → intestinal metaplasia → adenocarcinoma

explanation.summary: The Correa cascade proceeds gastritis → metaplasia → dysplasia → cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: H. pylori-driven carcinogenesis follows: normal mucosa → chronic gastritis → intestinal metaplasia → dysplasia → adenocarcinoma. Chronic inflammation induces metaplasia, which acquires dysplasia and ultimately becomes invasive cancer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dysplasia cannot precede the chronic gastritis and metaplasia that generate it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chronic gastritis is the initiating step and must come before intestinal metaplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Adenocarcinoma is the endpoint, not the first step after normal mucosa.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Intestinal metaplasia precedes dysplasia; the order here is reversed.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man is diagnosed with a distal (antral) intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma involving the lower two-thirds of the stomach without distant metastasis. Which of the following is the most appropriate surgical management?

explanation.summary: Distal two-thirds lesions are treated with partial gastrectomy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Partial (subtotal) gastrectomy is used for lesions of the distal two-thirds of the stomach, whereas total gastrectomy is reserved for proximal-third lesions. This antral tumor is best managed with partial gastrectomy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: H. pylori eradication treats MALT lymphoma and reduces cancer risk but does not treat established adenocarcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Imatinib is for GISTs, not adenocarcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Endoscopic polypectomy treats small polyps, not invasive adenocarcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Total gastrectomy is reserved for proximal-third lesions, not distal antral tumors.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man is 2 years out from total gastrectomy for gastric adenocarcinoma. He now presents with fatigue, glossitis, and a macrocytic anemia with hypersegmented neutrophils. Deficiency of which nutrient is the most likely cause?

explanation.summary: Loss of parietal cells after gastrectomy causes B12 deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Post-gastrectomy complications include malabsorption of vitamin B12 (also calcium and iron). Loss of parietal cells eliminates intrinsic factor, causing B12 deficiency with macrocytic anemia, hypersegmented neutrophils, and glossitis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy, not macrocytic anemia after gastrectomy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Folate deficiency also causes macrocytic anemia, but the classic post-gastrectomy deficiency from loss of intrinsic factor is B12.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vitamin K deficiency causes bleeding from impaired clotting factors, not macrocytic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thiamine deficiency causes beriberi or Wernicke encephalopathy, not this megaloblastic picture.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man from East Asia is counseled about gastric cancer risk. Which of the following statements about the epidemiology and prognosis of gastric adenocarcinoma is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most people infected with H. pylori will develop gastric cancer

choices.label: B
choices.text: Early-stage gastric cancer has a 5-year survival above 90%, while advanced disease is below 30%

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gastric adenocarcinoma is more common in North America than in East Asia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Diets rich in fruits and vegetables increase the risk of gastric cancer

choices.label: E
choices.text: Early-stage gastric cancer characteristically produces severe, obvious symptoms

explanation.summary: Early gastric cancer has excellent survival; advanced disease is poor.
explanation.whyCorrect: Early-stage gastric cancer has a 5-year survival rate above 90%, whereas advanced disease has a survival below 30%. This underscores the value of early detection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Malignancy develops in only about 3% of those infected with H. pylori, not most.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gastric adenocarcinoma is roughly 20 times more common in high-risk regions like East Asia, not North America.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fruit and vegetable-rich diets are protective, not risk-increasing, likely due to antioxidants.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Early-stage disease is often asymptomatic, so patients frequently present at an advanced stage.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with cachexia and gastric adenocarcinoma is noted to have a firm, palpable nodule at the umbilicus. Biopsy confirms metastatic adenocarcinoma. This finding is best termed which of the following?

explanation.summary: A periumbilical metastatic nodule is a Sister Mary Joseph nodule.
explanation.whyCorrect: A Sister Mary Joseph nodule is a periumbilical metastasis of gastric (and other intra-abdominal) cancer, indicating advanced disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A Virchow node is a left supraclavicular lymph node metastasis, not periumbilical.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A Krukenberg tumor is ovarian metastasis from gastric cancer, not an umbilical nodule.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Blumer shelf refers to a palpable rectal shelf from pelvic drop metastases, not an umbilical nodule.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trousseau sign here refers to migratory thrombophlebitis associated with malignancy, not a periumbilical nodule.

questions.stem: A pathologist compares two resected gastric GISTs. Which combination of features best predicts a high risk of metastasis and recurrence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Size under 5 cm with low mitotic activity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Location in the stomach rather than small bowel

choices.label: D
choices.text: Size greater than 10 cm with high mitotic activity

explanation.summary: Large size and high mitotic rate predict aggressive GIST behavior.
explanation.whyCorrect: GISTs smaller than 5 cm have low metastasis and recurrence rates, while higher rates are seen in mitotically active lesions larger than 10 cm. Size and mitotic index are the key prognostic drivers.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Tumors under 5 cm with low mitotic activity have low risk, not high risk.
whyWrongByChoice.B: PDGFRA mutations tend to be associated with a more indolent course, not high risk by themselves.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gastric location is generally more favorable than small bowel GISTs, not a high-risk feature.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CD117 positivity is a diagnostic marker present in most GISTs and does not by itself predict aggressiveness.

questions.stem: A researcher subtypes a gastric adenocarcinoma and finds it is Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) positive. Which molecular characteristic is most consistent with EBV-positive gastric adenocarcinoma?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Uniform signet ring cell morphology with linitis plastica

choices.label: D
choices.text: Arising from a familial adenomatous polyposis background

explanation.summary: EBV-positive gastric cancers characteristically lack TP53 mutations.
explanation.whyCorrect: EBV is associated with about 10% of gastric adenocarcinomas, and these tumors lack TP53 mutations, suggesting a distinct pathogenesis driven by the virus rather than classic TP53 inactivation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: KIT gain-of-function mutations characterize GISTs, not EBV-positive adenocarcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CDH1 germline mutation defines hereditary diffuse gastric cancer, not the EBV subtype.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Signet ring cells and linitis plastica define diffuse-type cancer, which is a separate entity from the EBV subtype.
whyWrongByChoice.D: FAP predisposes to intestinal-type gastric cancer, not specifically the EBV-associated subtype.
